parts.text: In England, all initial teacher education providers are inspected by Ofsted. In other nations, accreditation inspections may be conducted by professional

bodies, such as the Teaching Council of Ireland. Across these different systems, many academics described feeling anticipatory stress while waiting for an inspection.

Participants in England described living in “

anticipation”, on “constant red alert” and “on a knife edge” while waiting for the call from Ofsted.

The inspection had not begun, but the expectation of it was already shaping how they worked, where they directed their attention and even how

they could make plans outside work. As one participant said, “every family plan is prefaced with, ‘but I could get the call’”.

Anticipation itself is not the problem. It’s a normal psychological function that allows us to prepare for what is

. The difficulty arises when we know something important is approaching, but our personal control is limited, and we don’t have enough information to decide what useful preparation actually looks like.

Under those conditions, the mind keeps working on the problem. We

possible outcomes, we revisit conversations we have had and we can become more attentive to potential signals.

An unexpected request for a meeting or a delayed email response can suddenly acquire particular

, not necessarily because it means anything, but because uncertainty can make us more vigilant for information that might help predict what comes next.

Psychologists use the term “perseverative cognition” to describe how worry and rumination can keep a potential

mentally active when it is not actually present. In simple terms, the stressful event may be absent, but the mind keeps bringing it back into the present.

As one of my interviewees explained: “My mind has already gone into

with worry – even though the inspection might not take place until next year.” Another said: “It’s the ‘not knowing’ that I find so stressful.” Indeed, research into uncertain threat suggests that unpredictability can sustain vigilance,

because there is no clear point at which we know we can safely stand down.

Stressful events at work

Many of the events we anticipate at work also carry an element of evaluation. An inspection, promotion process or performance review can place our
directly under scrutiny, while restructuring may raise a broader question about our future value within an organisation.
